theory.heading: Identify the visual feature
theory.body: An evidence-based aesthetic judgement begins by identifying a feature that can be seen. This might include texture, pattern, symmetry, contrast, layout, geometric form, organic form, visual hierarchy or emphasis. Describe the feature precisely rather than making a general comment. For example, a student might notice repeated shapes, balanced spacing or one feature that appears more prominent than the others. Do not invent the colour, finish, emblem or other details of a particular Footstool. Base the description only on the visual evidence available.

theory.heading: Name the aesthetic criterion
theory.body: Next, connect the feature to an appropriate aesthetic criterion. A repeated arrangement relates to pattern, noticeable difference relates to contrast, and the order in which elements attract attention relates to visual hierarchy. The criterion gives the observation a clear focus and helps explain why the feature matters. Avoid using several terms without showing how they apply. A strong judgement links one visible feature to a criterion that accurately describes it.

theory.heading: Explain the effect on the viewer
theory.body: Finish by explaining how the feature may affect the viewer. A central feature with strong contrast may attract attention first, while repeated elements may create unity or rhythm. Balanced spacing may make a layout appear organised. Use cautious language because viewers can respond differently. Evidence-based analysis explains the visual reason for a response, while a comment such as I like it gives only personal preference. Current school SOPs and teacher directions control all actual workshop activity. When the intended effect is uncertain, describe the observed effect without claiming to know the designer's intention.

questions.question: What should begin an evidence-based aesthetic judgement?
choices: A claim about the designer's intention
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. A strong judgement begins with a feature that can be directly observed.
questions.retryFeedback: Review Identify the visual feature and focus on the first step in the analysis.

questions.question: Which statement is a precise visual observation?
choices: Repeated shapes appear across the layout
The finish must be high quality
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. This statement identifies an observable feature without adding unsupported details.
questions.retryFeedback: Return to Identify the visual feature and focus on the difference between observation and general opinion.

questions.question: What should a student avoid when visual details are not available?
choices: Inventing the actual colour or finish
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Analysis must use available evidence rather than invented product details.
questions.retryFeedback: Re-read Identify the visual feature and identify the details that must not be assumed.

questions.question: Which criterion best matches a noticeable difference between visual elements?
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Contrast describes a noticeable difference between visual elements.
questions.retryFeedback: Review Name the aesthetic criterion and focus on the criterion linked to visual difference.

questions.question: Which criterion describes the order in which elements attract attention?
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Visual hierarchy describes what a viewer notices first, second and later.
questions.retryFeedback: Return to Name the aesthetic criterion and identify the term linked to viewing order.

questions.question: Why should an aesthetic term be linked to a visible feature?
choices: To show accurately how the criterion applies
To prove the design is successful
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Linking the term to evidence shows why the criterion is relevant.
questions.retryFeedback: Re-read Name the aesthetic criterion and focus on what makes a judgement well supported.

questions.question: Which statement best explains an effect on the viewer?
choices: The designer wanted everyone to feel impressed
The larger central feature may attract attention first
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. This connects an observable feature to a cautious explanation of its visual effect.
questions.retryFeedback: Review Explain the effect on the viewer and focus on how visual impact should be described.
questions.theoryAnchor: Explain the effect on the viewer

questions.question: Why is the comment I like it not enough for aesthetic analysis?
choices: It does not explain the visual evidence behind the response
It proves the design has failed
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Analysis must explain which feature and criterion created the response.
questions.retryFeedback: Return to Explain the effect on the viewer and compare personal preference with evidence-based analysis.
questions.theoryAnchor: Explain the effect on the viewer

questions.question: How should a student describe an uncertain visual effect?
choices: State the designer's intention as fact
Use cautious language based on what is visible
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Cautious wording recognises that visual responses may differ between viewers.
questions.retryFeedback: Re-read Explain the effect on the viewer and focus on how uncertainty should be handled.
questions.theoryAnchor: Explain the effect on the viewer

questions.question: Which sequence forms a complete aesthetic judgement?
choices: Visible feature, aesthetic criterion and effect on the viewer
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. A complete judgement identifies evidence, names the relevant criterion and explains its visual effect.
questions.retryFeedback: Review all of Explain the effect on the viewer and identify the three connected parts of the analysis.
questions.theoryAnchor: Explain the effect on the viewer

written.prompt: Write one evidence-based aesthetic judgement that identifies a visible feature, names an aesthetic criterion and explains its possible effect on the viewer.
written.sentenceStarter: The visible feature is ___. This relates to ___ because ___. It may affect the viewer by ___.
written.example: The visible feature is a larger central shape surrounded by smaller repeated forms. This relates to visual hierarchy because the size difference creates a clear viewing order. It may cause the viewer to notice the central shape first.
